ts-reserved-field-names

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

Genus fields, methods, variant fields, parameters and locals may be spelled like ECMAScript reserved words; a field is read, written and built under the name it was declared with.

Syntax: class Pouch { var int yield; fn delete(int await) → int { const int let ← await + self.yield; return let } }

Category#

identifier

Related#

  • keyword-as-ident
  • rust-reserved-names

Examples#

radix/corpus/keyword-as-ident/ts-reserved-field-names.fab (canonical · concept)#

Genus fields, methods, variant fields, parameters and locals may be spelled like ECMAScript reserved words; a field is read, written and built under the name it was declared with.

# =============================================================================
# ts-reserved-field-names — property names that look like JavaScript keywords
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • `yield`, `delete`, `default`, `new`, `await`, `let`, `static`, `enum`,
#     `implements`, `interface`, `package`, `private`, `protected` and `public`
#     are ordinary identifiers in Faber. A class field or method, a union
#     variant field, a parameter and a local may all use them.
#   • A field keeps one spelling on every backend: the name it was declared
#     with is the name it is read, written, constructed and displayed under.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Renaming a field to dodge a target's reserved word — the compiler keeps
#     the property name and only escapes bindings (locals, parameters).
#
# See also: keyword-as-ident, rust-reserved-names
# =============================================================================

# ts-reserved-field-names — reserved-word spellings as fields, methods, variant fields and bindings
#
# EXPECTED OUTPUT:
#   ts-reserved-field-names.expected — the computed values, then the displayed class.

class Pouch {
    var int yield
    var int delete
    var int default
    var int static
    var int enum
    var int implements
    var int interface
    var int package
    var int private
    var int protected
    var int public

    fn new(int await) → int {
        const int let ← await + self.yield
        return let + self.delete + self.default
    }

    fn function() → int {
        return self.static + self.enum + self.implements + self.interface
    }

    fn visibility() → int {
        return self.package + self.private + self.protected + self.public
    }
}

union Shift {
    Move {
        int yield
        int delete
    },
    Stay
}

fn pack(int yield, int default) → int {
    return yield + default
}

fn weigh(Shift s) → int {
    match s {
        case Move const yield, delete {
            return yield * 10 + delete
        }
        case Stay {
            return 0
        }
    }
}

main {
    const Pouch b ← Pouch { yield = 1, delete = 2, default = 3, static = 4, enum = 5, implements = 6, interface = 7, package = 8, private = 9, protected = 10, public = 11 }
    print b.yield
    print b.delete
    print b.default
    print b.new(10)
    print b.function()
    print b.visibility()
    print pack(1, 2)

    var Pouch c ← Pouch { yield = 4, delete = 5, default = 6, static = 0, enum = 0, implements = 0, interface = 0, package = 0, private = 0, protected = 0, public = 0 }
    c.yield ← 9
    c.delete ← c.delete + 1
    print c.yield + c.delete

    const Shift moved ← variant Move { yield = 3, delete = 4 } ∷ Shift
    print weigh(moved)
    print weigh(variant Stay ∷ Shift)

    # Destructuring reads the properties and binds escaped local names.
    from b const yield, delete as new
    print yield
    print new

    print b
}

Expected output:

1
2
3
16
22
38
3
15
34
0
1
2
Pouch { yield = 1, delete = 2, default = 3, static = 4, enum = 5, implements = 6, interface = 7, package = 8, private = 9, protected = 10, public = 11 }
